sentences.text: The MIT AI Risk Repository is a database of more than 1,700 AI risks extracted from published risk frameworks, run by the MIT AI Risk Initiative (MIT FutureTech) (MMRS record); its own page gives it three parts, an AI Risk Database that "captures 1700+ risks extracted from 74 existing frameworks and classifications of AI risks", a Causal Taxonomy and a Domain Taxonomy, and the Initiative's home page calls it a "living repository of AI risks".

Its unit is the risk as a framework states it (MMRS record), "risk, extracted from published risk frameworks" in the record's field, each risk linked to "the source information (paper title, authors) and supporting evidence, such as quotes and page numbers" (MIT IDE), and each source framework summarized with its source documents and key excerpts published (MMRS record), as the home page's deck of the 65 Version 3 frameworks gives them.

Its report post of April 2025 calls it "a structured and evolving resource" consolidating how AI risks are categorized across academic, industry and policy literatures, its LinkedIn page "a comprehensive living database of over 1000 AI risks categorized by their cause and risk domain", and the Initiative's file for machines names /risks its canonical page, with "methodology notes, use cases, limitations, data access links, and citation guidance".

Slattery and colleagues start from terminology: "researchers, policymakers, and technology companies lack shared terminology for discussing AI risks", so that "privacy" names a model's ability to leak sensitive training data in one framework and freedom from government surveillance in another (arXiv:2408.12622, v3).

The Initiative offers "Authoritative data and frameworks to help you identify, prioritize, and manage the risks from AI" (home page); the v1 abstract calls the repository, to its authors' knowledge, "the first attempt to rigorously curate, analyze, and extract AI risk frameworks into a publicly accessible, comprehensive, extensible, and categorized risk database", and the published article's snippet promises "concrete tools for managing AI's societal impact across multiple stakeholder[s]" (ScienceDirect card).

The MMRS record reads the same object as an aggregator of aggregators, "its sources are frameworks, which are themselves syntheses": "What enters is what a framework named", and "A risk no framework has written down has no row"; the repository's FAQ states the boundary as its limit, 65 documents from more than 17,000 records screened, which "May be missing emerging, domain-specific risks, and unpublished risks", and a framework can itself reach back to events, as the taxonomy of generative AI failures built from 499 publicly reported incidents that Version 4 added (December 2025 update).

Its method is "a systematic review of taxonomies and other structured classifications of AI risk followed by an expert consultation", its taxonomies made by "a best-fit framework synthesis" (v1 abstract), restated in the FAQ as a systematic search with forwards and backwards searching and expert consultation that identified 65 documents and extracted 1600+ risks; there are two taxonomies because causal categories such as "Diffusion of responsibility" do not map to hazard categories such as "Misuse" (FAQ).

The Causal Taxonomy classifies each risk by Entity (Human, AI), Intentionality (Intentional, Unintentional) and Timing (Pre-deployment, Post-deployment) (v1 abstract), and the repository's page gives each factor a third value, "Other: Due to some other reason or ambiguous" for entity.

The Domain Taxonomy sorts risks into seven domains, discrimination and toxicity, privacy and security, misinformation, malicious actors and misuse, human-computer interaction, socioeconomic and environmental, and AI system safety, failures and limitations (v1 abstract), each with subdomains (MMRS record): 23 in v1, 24 on the repository's page, 25 in the April 2025 report post, the subdomain for multi-agent risks added in April 2025 (MMRS record; report post).

Its v3 finding is that, "contrary to common assumptions, human decisions cause nearly as many AI risks (38%) as the AI systems themselves (42%)" (arXiv v3); the first release had found 51% of risks caused by AI systems and 34% by humans, 65% after deployment and 10% before, and Slattery gave as its key finding "the average framework covering only 34% of the identified risk subdomains and even the most significant frameworks covering only 70%" (MIT IDE).

The counts are versioned: 777 risks from 43 frameworks at the first release, "A new MIT FutureTech project" (MIT IDE, 21 August 2024), "777 risks extracted from 43 taxonomies" in the v1 abstract; 22 frameworks added to 65 documents and 1,612 unique risk entries in April 2025 (report post); Version 4 live on 4 December 2025 with 9 frameworks and about 200 risk categories added, "over 1,700 coded risks" (December 2025 update); and "74 frameworks containing 1,725 distinct risks" in v3 of the paper, repeated on the repository's page as 1700+ from 74.

Older figures stand beside the current one on the Initiative's own pages: "1,700+ AI risks from 65 frameworks" on the home page, "more than 1,600 risks from more than 65 frameworks and papers" and, further down the same About page, "1700+ risks from 70+ frameworks", and "more than 1,700" in the LinkedIn post; the MMRS record gives "more than 1,700 risks from 65 frameworks" as of 2026-10-28, read from airisk.mit.edu for "scope, version", with lifecycle "version 4, December 2025" (MMRS record).

The Capture Registry takes 1,700 from 65 as the record's count for version 4 and finds that, of the three sizes on the cards, "the composition gives the current one" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29); version 4's post adds 9 frameworks to version 3's 65, and v3 of the paper and the repository's page give 74 while the home page gives 65, so the record's 65 is held beside the 74, each with its source.

Its stated limits are "a single expert reviewer for extraction and coding", risks extracted as presented, poorly communicated ones included, and taxonomies that "prioritize clarity and simplicity over nuance" and do not categorize risks by impact, likelihood or their interaction (repository FAQ); Slattery expected it to "need some modification before it is useful for most audiences" (MIT IDE).

The MMRS record lists extraction method and licence as unchecked; the field states both, the method above and "Data from the MIT AI Risk Initiative is licensed under CC BY 4.0" (home page), "most of our outputs are published under a CC BY 4.0 licence" (About page), "Our Database is free to copy and use" (repository page), the paper CC BY 4.0 in Patterns (arXiv).

Its operator is the MIT AI Risk Initiative (AIRI), "based at MIT FutureTech, a joint initiative of the Institute of the Digital Economy and MIT CSAIL" (About page), as the MMRS record gives it, on the operator's statement.

Its paper is by Peter Slattery, Alexander K. Saeri, Emily A. C. Grundy, Jess Graham, Michael Noetel, Risto Uuk, James Dao, Soroush Pour, Stephen Casper and Neil Thompson, submitted on 14 August 2024 and revised to v3 on 5 May 2026 (arXiv), with versions of August 2024 and April 2025 (report post), published in Patterns (Cell Press, 2026), and the repository asks to be cited by its preprint (FAQ).

The repository is one of the Initiative's "several connected workstreams, each answering a different question", beside an AI Incident Tracker "Developed in collaboration with the AI Incident Database" (About page), which the Initiative's LinkedIn post calls "a collaboration with the Responsible AI Collaborative, which connects risks to over 1,400 incidents".

The MMRS record keeps the incidents apart from the risks, "real-world incidents are kept separately in its AI Incident Tracker", records the tracker as part of the repository, classifying AI Incident Database reports against the same taxonomy through Arcola AI's language-model pipeline, and reads that layer as "a second-order reading of the AI Incident Database, done by machine" (MMRS record); the field's About page sets the tracker beside the repository as a workstream, and the two placements stand each with its source.

In the record's harm basin the repository "sits over the harm basin as a taxonomy for it", its role harm and its neighbour the AI Incident Database, whose own record says the repository "aggregates risk frameworks over the same ground and keeps its own incident tracker" (MMRS record); the repository's FAQ names as other databases of AI risks MITRE ATT&CK, airisk.io, AVID and aitracker.org.

The MIT AI Risk Navigator, "A project of the AI Risk Initiative at MIT FutureTech" with the support of the Cambridge Boston Alignment Initiative, connects the repository's datasets "through a shared taxonomy" and says of itself "This is a research prototype. The data and analyses are preliminary and not yet validated" (its home page); the Capture Registry finds it "a third MIT surface" while "the census holds the repository and the tracker", "Added as a candidate", and the MMRS record lists it as a candidate to enter "once it has been read at its own pages", a distinct entity.

The Initiative publishes a file "to orient LLMs and AI agents" that asks them to "Refer to the project as the MIT AI Risk Initiative", to "Check the linked pages before giving exact counts, dates, version numbers, or coverage claims", to "distinguish reported incidents from predicted risks", to note that the Navigator "is a research prototype", and not to present the datasets "as legal, safety, or investment advice" (llms.txt).

Its About page counts 250+ citations, the 2025 and 2026 International AI Safety Reports among them, and 290,000+ website users, and calls the site "One of the top sources returned for search queries on AI risks and incidents"; in its first week over 35,000 people used the website (MIT IDE).

The MMRS record has "two nodes, the MMRS record and the entity it describes", each assertion with a source and a basis and the lifecycle "kept apart from the observation that saw it", and it links the capture as "the composition layer's account of the entity, seated in the Capture Registry" (MMRS record).

At the entity's name the Capture Registry finds "The repository is composed at a finer grain than the record holds, its taxonomy named domain by domain", the seven domains and the causal taxonomy "the record's 'domain taxonomy with subdomains' given at full grain", checked against the record and the entity's own pages on 2026-10-29 (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).
